claims.text: Brittle behavior in compositionally complex high-entropy alloys emerges when grain-boundary segregation and nanoscale precipitate formation reach a critical threshold during thermal exposure.
Grain-boundary segregation and nanoscale precipitates reduce grain-boundary cohesion.
Reduced grain-boundary cohesion shifts fracture from ductile to brittle while the bulk matrix remains single-phase.
The initial alloy is single-phase and compositionally complex, with nearly homogeneous grain-boundary chemistry.
Controlled service-like thermal aging can promote grain-boundary segregation and nanoscale precipitation without significant grain coarsening.
Thermal aging produces local grain-boundary compositional changes that nucleate nanoscale intergranular precipitates.
Thermally induced grain-boundary segregation fosters brittle intermetallic precipitation at grain boundaries.
Intergranular brittle precipitates promote brittle fracture by reducing intergranular cohesion.
Thermally aged samples will have lower toughness than the initially homogenously processed alloy.
Thermal aging will shift fracture from ductile transgranular fracture toward brittle intergranular fracture.
Thermally aged samples will show lower ductility and fracture resistance than the baseline.
The as-processed baseline has minimal grain-boundary segregation, no significant intergranular precipitates, and high ductility and toughness.
The proposed mechanism is limited to exposures sufficient to cause grain-boundary segregation but not overall grain coarsening or extensive bulk intermetallic growth.
The embrittlement thresholds for segregant concentration and precipitate volume fraction depend on alloy composition and environmental loading conditions.
